summary.text: 生 is analyzed as a sprout emerging from the ground. Oracle-bone examples use it for childbirth and living things, among other senses, but do not establish which use came first or that all later meanings developed from the pictured plant.

formation.text: A semantic compound with pictorial parts: 屮 depicts a sprout and 一 represents the ground beneath it. Neither part is proposed as a sound cue. In later forms, a mark added beneath 屮 developed into a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土.

components.text: Within 生, 屮 depicts the sprout rising above ground. It contributes to the plant image; no phonetic role is proposed.

In the early graphic analysis, 一 represents the ground beneath the sprout. A later mark added below 屮 developed into a horizontal stroke, making the lower part resemble 土; 土 is not identified as the original component.

history.text: The selected oracle-bone-style and Western Zhou bronze-style renderings illustrate the sprout-over-ground design. The graphic account describes early bronze forms as retaining this structure, then a mark beneath the sprout developing into a horizontal stroke. These are modern vector renderings, and the account does not supply a dated sequence of individual artifacts.

The historical dictionary account describes plants emerging above soil and glosses 生 as “advance.” A later graphic interpretation treats “advance” as an extended sense rather than the image’s core meaning.

生 was also used to write 姓, “surname.” This proposed reuse of the whole graph writes a different word, potentially because the words sounded alike or similarly; it does not show a change in 生’s meaning. One oracle-bone phrase is read 多生, though 多甥 is an alternative. Modern Mandarin readings are shēng and xìng; supplied Middle Chinese forms are sraeng and sjengH, but these comparisons do not establish an ancient sound match or borrowing.

uncertainties.text: The oracle-bone phrase 生月 has been read as “following month,” but “this month” and other readings have also been proposed. Its meaning and any relation to life or growth remain unsettled.

Early reported uses include childbirth, live or fresh animals, and 生月; other examples include living, lifespan, and producing or occurring. The examples do not date every use or establish an ordered development among these senses.
A conservative form 𤯓 is mentioned, but the evidence here does not establish its chronology or ancestry, or whether its shape resulted from corruption.

senses.text: 生 is reported in an oracle-bone prayer for childbirth. Other early uses are also reported, so this does not establish childbirth as the character’s first meaning.
生 is reported as an adjective describing live animals in oracle-bone inscriptions. This does not establish its priority relative to the childbirth use.
One interpretation reads 生月 as “following month,” but other readings are contested. This phrase does not establish a semantic development from plant growth.
生 is reported as an adjective for fresh or live animals; separate historical phonology entries record “fresh, raw.” No chronology connecting this sense to the others is established.
Bronze-inscription examples are reported with the sense “occur” or “produce.” The evidence does not show when or how this use developed from other senses.
A bronze-inscription example is reported with the sense “lifespan.” No transition from the other attested senses is established.
A historical dictionary glosses 生 as “advance”; a later interpretation treats this as an extended sense. The evidence does not date this sense or show its development.

senses.period: Warring States manuscripts and later usage
senses.text: A Warring States manuscript uses 生 for living in opposition to dying. Later lexicographic evidence also records life and living, without establishing a complete development from earlier uses.

limitations.text: The inscription examples support several uses but do not establish priority or a securely dated chain among birth, living, freshness, production, lifespan, advance, and life.
The proposed sprout-and-ground image does not by itself show that every recorded word meaning developed from plant growth.
The “following month” reading of 生月 is disputed and does not demonstrate a semantic transition from growth or life to month terminology.

overview.text: 生 pictures a sprout emerging from the ground. Early inscriptions also use it for childbirth and living things, but do not establish which use came first.

components.text: 屮 depicts the sprout rising above the ground line.
一 represents the ground beneath the sprout.

relationships.text: Within 生, 屮 depicts the sprout in the sprout-emerging-from-ground image.
Within the early analysis of 生, 一 represents the ground beneath the depicted sprout.
